excerpts.text: This is an exposition of the classical BLVZ chessboard bound , not a new connectivity theorem. Work with reduced homology over \(\mathbb F_2\). Call a complex \(q\)-acyclic when its reduced homology vanishes from degree \(-1\) through \(q\); \((-1)\)-acyclic means it has a vertex, and conditions below \(-1\) are vacuous.

Homological cover lemma. Suppose a finite complex \(K\) is covered by subcomplexes \(L_1,\ldots,L_t\), their nerve is \(q\)-acyclic, and every nonempty intersection of \(s\) members is \((q-s+1)\)-acyclic, where \(q\ge0\). Then \(K\) is \(q\)-acyclic.

Vertically first, the first page is \(\bigoplus_{|J|=a+1}H_b(L_J)\). Its groups with \(b>0\), \(a+b\le q\), vanish by the intersection hypotheses. For \(b=0\), \(a\le q\), every nonempty intersection is connected, so the remaining horizontal groups and maps are the nerve chain complex. At \(a=q+1\), the augmentation \(H_0(L_J)\to\mathbb F_2\) is still onto; hence the incoming boundaries contain all nerve boundaries needed in degree \(q\). The second page has zero reduced groups in total degrees at most \(q\). Later pages cannot create nonzero groups from zero entries, and the finite filtration converges. Augmenting degree zero gives the asserted reduced-homology vanishing. \(\square\)

Proof by the standard star cover. Transpose so \(a\le b\) and induct on \(a\). If \(\nu=1\), nonemptiness suffices. Otherwise \(q=\nu-2\ge0\) and \(a\ge2\). Cover by the closed stars of the row-one vertices \((1,j)\). They are cones. A matching avoiding row one uses at most \(a-1<b\) columns, so it belongs to some star. An intersection of \(s\ge2\) stars is \(\Delta_{a-1,b-s}\), on the remaining rows and columns. Every proper subfamily has a vertex in its intersection, while the full intersection does not. The nerve is the boundary of a \((b-1)\)-simplex, a sphere of dimension \(b-2\).
